item.title: Components and assemblies
item.description:
One definition, several occurrences 

from scpf import Box, assembly, component

@component
class Beam:
 length = 100.0

 def build(self):
 return Box(self.length, 20, 20)

@assembly
class BeamPair:
 spacing = 120.0

 def build(self):
 left = Beam()
 right = left.copy(placement=Placement(x=self.spacing))
 return (left + right).group("Beams")

pair = BeamPair()

@component marks one reusable physical part. Its build() returns the complete geometry/feature tree for that part; that tree may be made from many primitives and features. @assembly marks a class whose build() composes separate component occurrences. Both decorators return callable model objects, so normal model code stays readable as Beam() and BeamPair().

SolidCraft receives one reusable definition and multiple occurrences. A group is a native parent component in the browser, not a Boolean fusion of its children.

Component parameter visibility

Reusable component defaults are fixed by default. Publish selected child parameters explicitly with include=:

@component(include=("inside_corner_radius",))
class CornerBracket:
 width = 24.0
 inside_corner_radius = 4.0

 def build(self):
 ...

When a parent Parameter or expression is passed into a child input, that existing dependency stays symbolic. For example, CornerBracket(inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius) reuses the parent design’s corner_radius; it does not create a separate CornerBracket_inside_corner_radius parameter.

Occurrence placement

copy() retains the source Placement when no override is supplied. copy(placement=Placement(...)) creates the new occurrence with the supplied absolute pose in the parent coordinate frame. The compiler uses creation-time copy translation where SolidCraft can represent it and a native fallback only where required.

center = BeamComponent()
array = center
for x in (-240, -120, 120, 240):
 array = array + center.copy(placement=Placement(x=x))

Component attachment 

right = BeamComponent().attach(
 left, parent=Anchor.RIGHT, child=Anchor.LEFT
)

marker = Marker().attach(
 frame,
 parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_RIGHT,
 child=Anchor.BACK_TOP_RIGHT,
)

attach() is the public Forge relationship between reusable components. Anchor selects the attachment reference: a supported face, or one of the eight rectangular corners such as FRONT_TOP_RIGHT. Corner anchors compile to native SolidCraft edge/corner origins, so they follow dimension changes in a saved design.

Associative in-plane attachment offset

attach(offset=(u, v)) moves the child within the attachment plane. Numeric values and parameter expressions are both supported. Forge lowers a non-zero or symbolic in-plane offset to a native planar joint and keeps u and v as SolidCraft joint values, so they are re-evaluated when their parameters change.

wood = Parameter("wood_thickness", 18)

bracket = Bracket().attach(
 side,
 parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT,
 child=mount,
 offset=(0, -wood + 12),
 gap=-12,
)

offset is independent of gap: the two offset values move in the attachment plane, while gap remains the normal distance between the two references. On a rectangular corner origin, the second planar value follows the selected vertical corner edge; its sign is defined by that corner frame rather than by world Z.

Assembly-owned named anchors

When a datum belongs to the meaning of an assembly rather than to a generic component, keep it on the assembly with with_anchor(). The anchor stores the target occurrence plus its attachment reference. Consumers resolve it by name with anchor().

frame = (left + right + bottom).with_anchor(
 "front_top_left",
 left,
 AnchorTopology(
 edge=(-6, 0, 181),
 on=(0, 0, 181),
 corner=(-6, 0, 362),
 z=(0, 0, -1),
 x=(1, 0, 0),
 ),
)

parent = frame.anchor("front_top_left")
bracket = CornerBracket().attach(
 parent.target,
 parent=parent.reference,
 child=bracket_reference,
)

This keeps a generic Board or CornerBracket free of application-specific anchor names while a higher-level frame can expose semantic datums such as front_top_left.

An assembly anchor may also carry its own symbolic offset=(u, v). Consumers can combine that semantic offset with a fixed local correction and pass the result to attach(offset=...). This is useful when an assembly datum follows a frame parameter such as wall thickness while the reusable part keeps a fixed mounting correction.

AnchorFrame: point plus orientation

An AnchorFrame describes one local attachment coordinate frame. origin gives the local point; z gives the attachment normal and x fixes the rotation around that normal. Use it when a single point or rectangular Anchor is not enough to describe how the occurrence must be oriented.

from scpf import Anchor, AnchorFrame

mount = AnchorFrame(
 origin=(0, 0, -12),
 z=(0, 1, 0),
 x=(0, 0, -1),
)

bracket = CornerBracket().attach(
 side_board,
 parent=Anchor.FRONT_TOP_LEFT,
 child=mount,
)

There are two ownership patterns. If the datum is an intrinsic part of a reusable component, expose it with anchors() and refer to it by name. If the frame exists only because of a particular assembly or mounting choice, construct the AnchorFrame in that assembly and pass it directly to attach(). This keeps application knowledge out of the generic component definition.

@component
class Sensor:
 def anchors(self):
 return {
 "connector": AnchorFrame(
 origin=(12, 0, 4),
 z=(1, 0, 0),
 x=(0, 0, 1),
 )
 }

 def build(self):
 return Box(24, 12, 8)

sensor = Sensor().attach(panel, child="connector")

For an unrotated occurrence, Forge lowers an AnchorFrame directly into the native joint.create reference as point, z and x; it does not create a persistent visible joint.origin. Named frames on explicitly rotated occurrences currently use the native origin fallback so SolidCraft owns the transform. A direct AnchorFrame on an explicitly rotated occurrence is not supported yet.

AnchorTopology: follow an edge or corner

AnchorTopology is a named component datum that stays attached to native SolidCraft topology. edge picks an edge, on selects its adjacent planar face and corner optionally chooses one endpoint. The coordinates are selection picks; SolidCraft keeps the selected edge, face and endpoint by topology name as the design changes.

from scpf import AnchorTopology, Box, component

@component
class Board:
 def anchors(self):
 return {
 "mount": AnchorTopology(
 edge=(-20, 50, 5),
 on=(-20, 50, 10),
 corner=(-20, 0, 5),
 z=(0, 1, 0),
 x=(0, 0, 1),
 )
 }

 def build(self):
 return Box(40, 100, 20)

This is useful for references such as the straight tangent edge beside a fillet: if dimensions move that edge, the joint can follow it without freezing the original XYZ point. The current implementation supports named or direct AnchorTopology values on non-rotated occurrences. A direct topology anchor is useful when the datum belongs only to one assembly rather than to the reusable component. SCPF deliberately does not transform topology picks itself.

SolidCraft joints remain an internal implementation detail; Forge does not expose a separate public Joint object.

What to test in an assembly

Check the native command list for one component.create per shared definition, expected occurrence.copy counts, and native translate, axis and angle parameters for rotated occurrences. Separately verify native SolidCraft geometry and its bounding dimensions before trusting an assembly image.

item.title: Drawings
item.description:
Forge can attach a native SolidCraft technical drawing to a completed design. Drawing intent is presentation state: keep it out of reusable component definitions and add it only when the part or assembly you want to document is complete.

Add a drawing to one component 

@component
class SamplePlate:
 def build(self):
 return Box(80, 50, 8, anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM)

part = SamplePlate().with_drawing(name="Sample Plate Drawing")

with_drawing() uses SolidCraft’s native iso-a4-part template by default and sets its first sheet to landscape. SolidCraft owns the paper, title block, standard front/top/right/isometric view layout and fitted scale. Forge binds the native drawing, component, occurrence, source, sheet and view identities returned by SolidCraft rather than predicting browser ids.

A4 by default, A3 when you ask for it 

part.with_drawing(
 name="Large assembly detail",
 template="iso-a3-part",
)

A4 landscape is the normal part-drawing default. Select A3 explicitly when the design needs more sheet area; the chosen native paper size is preserved and the sheet remains landscape. Forge does not silently switch an A3 request back to A4.

Document one component from an assembly 

assembly = left + right
assembly = assembly.with_drawing(
 left,
 name="Left bracket",
)

The selected occurrence must already belong to the completed Assembly. Projected views inherit the selected native occurrence subtree. Drawing intent does not alter normal occurrence placement or duplicate the reusable component definition.

Drawing intent versus published artifacts

Forge stores the native drawing in model.sc and declares the drawing artifact. The SCPF builder reopens that saved design and uses SolidCraft’s native drawing.export command twice: a vector PDF for publication and a 144 dpi PNG of the replay-bound sheet for static visual evidence. Forge model code does not embed repository or build-root paths.

build/<scope>/models/sample-plate-drawing/scpf/
 model.sc
 drawings/
 Sample-Plate-Drawing.pdf
 Sample-Plate-Drawing.png

Pages loads only the static PNG preview and exposes explicit Open PDF / Download PDF actions. It does not embed the PDF viewer on page load and copies neither generated artifact into gh-pages. See the Sample Plate Drawing example for the complete source, generated SolidCraft sequence, native model and drawing PDF.

Current drawing scope

The patch-qualified drawing slice covers native landscape part sheets, standard views, vector PDF publication and a native static sheet preview. Dimensions, notes, title-block authoring overrides, explicit view placement, balloons and parts lists remain separate future authoring capabilities. They will be evaluated against a real downstream Wall Hook drawing after this patch rather than being hidden as example-specific behavior.

item.title: Features and references
item.description:
A feature changes an existing body

A native feature is different from subtracting arbitrary CSG geometry. SCPF can retain named sketches and operations in SolidCraft history. For exact results, supported body types and selection constraints matter.

Holes 

from scpf import Box, Hole, Depth, Faces

plate = Box(100, 60, 10)
hole = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL)
plate = plate + hole.on(plate, face=Faces.TOP)

A Hole is a native hole feature: adding it to the shape means adding the operation that removes material. Faces.TOP selects its entry face. Simple feature placement uses on(); assembly attachment uses explicit anchors.

Native feature patterns

Pattern an already-applied native feature when the copies should remain one editable SolidCraft history operation. Rectangular and circular patterns share the same source-feature rules: pass the same Forge Shape object that was applied to the body. Forge resolves that object to its native history feature; callers never manage SolidCraft timeline-name strings. Direct native Hole-family and primitive features are supported alongside the existing Sketch.extrude() path, and a direct count Parameter remains editable in the saved design.

from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Hole

plate = Box(100, 80, 6, anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM)
bolt_hole = Hole(
 d=8,
 direction=(0, 0, -1),
).at(30, 0, 6)
plate = plate + bolt_hole

bolt_circle = plate.circular_pattern(
 bolt_hole,
 count=6,
 axis=Axis.Z,
)

circular_pattern() omits angle by default so SolidCraft uses its native 360-degree full-circle behaviour. Supply a fixed degree value or direct Parameter for a partial arc. origin=(x, y, z) moves a fixed axis; a fixed non-zero XYZ vector can be used instead of Axis.X/Y/Z. Construction-axis and geometry-axis selectors are not yet exposed by Forge.

grid = plate.rectangular_pattern(
 bolt_hole,
 count=4,
 spacing=20,
 direction=Axis.X,
 count2=3,
 spacing2=18,
 direction2=Axis.Y,
)

rectangular_pattern() and circular_pattern() both emit one native feature-pattern command rather than expanding independent copies in Python.

Fillets and chamfers 

from scpf import FRONT, LEFT, Box, Edges, Faces

body = Box(80, 50, 15)
top_perimeter = body.chamfer(
 1.5,
 edges=Edges.from_faces(Faces.TOP),
)
rounded = body.fillet(3, edges=Edges.VERTICAL)
one_edge = body.chamfer(3, edges=FRONT + LEFT)

fillet() and chamfer() use the same edge-selection forms. Prefer Edges.from_faces(...) when the intent is the complete boundary of named planar faces. Forge queries SolidCraft for those faces and their current edges during replay, then passes native {body,index} edge references to the modify feature; callers do not provide XYZ picks or predict topology ids.

with Sketch(plane="XZ") as profile:
 Polygon2D([(-20, 0), (20, 0), (20, 30), (-20, 30)],
 plane="XZ", world=True)

hook = profile.extrude(15, sym=True)
hook = hook.chamfer(
 1.5,
 edges=Edges.from_faces(Faces.FRONT, Faces.BACK),
)

Cardinal faces use world axes: TOP/BOTTOM are +/-Z, LEFT/RIGHT are -/+X, and FRONT/BACK are -/+Y. An XZ profile extrudes along Y, so its broad end faces are FRONT and BACK. Existing Edges.VERTICAL, two-direction Box selectors, Edges.from_profile(...), Edges.from_vertices(...) and explicit XYZ picks remain available for their existing contracts.

Shells 

from scpf import Box, Faces
case = Box(80, 50, 30).shell(2, open=Faces.TOP)

Faces.TOP chooses the face to open and is the same surface-selection vocabulary used by feature.on(...) and Edges.from_faces(...). Shell resolves the requested cardinal face through native SolidCraft topology before calling the native shell feature. Anchor is reserved for explicit component attachment in assemblies. See the source and regression tests for supported feature chains.

Feature placement without hard-coded global offsets 

from scpf import X, Y, Boss, Anchor

boss = Boss(d=7, h=12, hole_d=2.5).attach(
 case, parent=Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM,
 offset=(X.MIN + 10, Y.MAX - 10),
)

X.MIN and Y.MAX refer to the parent bounds and are not rotation-axis constants. Anchoring support currently focuses on rectangular bases and a documented set of faces. Do not assume every curved or lofted surface supports it.

item.title: From one component to an assembly
item.description:
Start with the mental model

Forge separates geometry from physical parts and from relationships between parts. Most assembly code becomes much easier once those three levels are kept separate.

You mean… Forge concept SolidCraft result
Geometry inside one part Shape Native geometry/features in one definition
One reusable physical part @component class Reusable component definition
Where/how one occurrence stands placement=Placement(...) Occurrence placement
One placed copy of that part Block() / copy() Component occurrence
Several parts collected together a + b Assembly containing occurrences
One part depends on another attach() Native SolidCraft assembly relationship/joint
A named mounting reference Anchor, AnchorFrame, AnchorTopology Reference used by that relationship
Browser/subassembly organisation group() Nested native component

1. A component means one physical part

A component is not limited to one primitive. It is the definition of one physical manufactured item. Its build() may contain several primitives, sketches, holes, bosses, fillets and other features as long as they together describe that one part.

from scpf import Box, Cylinder, component

@component
class MountingPlate:
 width = 80.0
 depth = 50.0
 thickness = 5.0

 def build(self):
 plate = Box(self.width, self.depth, self.thickness)
 boss = Cylinder(d=16, h=12).at(0, 0, self.thickness)
 return plate + boss

The plate and cylindrical boss are geometry/features inside one component. They do not need an assembly joint because they are not separate physical parts.

Physical-part test: if the boss is machined, printed or moulded as part of the plate, keep it inside one component. If it is actually a separate brass insert pressed into the plate, make a second component and relate the two occurrences in an assembly. MountingPlate is the reusable definition. Calling MountingPlate() creates one occurrence; copy() creates another occurrence of the same definition without duplicating the feature history.

2. Put components in one assembly 

first = Block(placement=Placement(x=-30))
second = first.copy(placement=Placement(x=30))

assembly = first + second

Here first + second means “these two component occurrences belong to one assembly”. It does not Boolean-union their solids.

Same operator, different level:Shape + Shape describes supported geometric union; occurrence + occurrence builds an assembly of physical parts. placement=Placement(...) declares the pose when an occurrence is created or copied. It does not create a mechanical relationship; use attach() when another occurrence owns the relationship.

Exploded views are presentation, not placement

Define an exploded view after composing the final assembly. Forge stores the view in SolidCraft without changing the occurrences’ normal Placement or joints.

assembly = first + second + third
assembly = assembly.with_exploded_view("Service", scale=1.25)
assembly = assembly.with_exploded_view(
 "Instructions",
 moves=[
 (second, (0, 25, 0)),
 (third, (0, 50, 10)),
 ],
)
assembly = assembly.show_assembled()

Automatic mode uses SolidCraft’s native scale-based explosion. Explicit mode takes occurrence objects and fixed XYZ translations; Forge resolves those objects to native occurrence ids during replay. Use show_exploded("Service") to display one stored view and show_assembled() to return to normal presentation. Do not model an explosion with ordinary occurrence moves.

Technical drawings are final design presentation

SolidCraft 0.49 can keep native drawing sheets inside the saved design. In Forge, drawing intent belongs to the completed design rather than to the reusable component definition.

left = Block()
right = left.copy(placement=Placement(x=40))

assembly = left + right
assembly = assembly.with_drawing(
 left,
 name="Block drawing",
)

For a standalone part, use Block().with_drawing(name="Block drawing"). Forge asks SolidCraft to create the native A4 part sheet and standard front, top, right and isometric views, then restricts those views to the selected occurrence. The sheet explicitly documents that component. A normal build also exports the drawing as a native vector PDF below drawings/. For a more complex part, pass template="iso-a3-part".

Layout stays native: Forge does not calculate paper coordinates or projected-view placement. SolidCraft owns the template, fitted scale and standard-view layout. In this first slice a part selected from a much larger assembly can therefore use a conservative scale, because SolidCraft fits the standard group before Forge narrows the view source. Dimensions, balloons, parts lists and other drawing annotations are outside this first API slice.

3. Use @assembly when the composition itself is reusable

You do not need @assembly merely because a script contains several components. Use it when the composition itself is a reusable model object that you want to import or instantiate as a subassembly.

from scpf import Anchor, assembly

@assembly
class BlockPair:
 def build(self):
 left = Block()
 right = Block().attach(
 left,
 parent=Anchor.RIGHT,
 child=Anchor.LEFT,
 )
 return left + right

pair = BlockPair()

The component definitions remain the physical parts. BlockPair describes how those occurrences are composed. This is different from group(): an assembly expresses the model composition; grouping controls the native nested hierarchy/browser unit.

4. Use attach() when the relationship is the intent

If the real rule is “the left side of this part belongs on the right side of that part”, encode that relationship instead of calculating a replacement XYZ coordinate yourself.

from scpf import Anchor

left = Block()
right = Block().attach(
 left,
 parent=Anchor.RIGHT,
 child=Anchor.LEFT,
)

assembly = left + right

Forge records an associative attachment between the two occurrences and lowers that to the native SolidCraft relationship mechanism. The anchors say which references are related; they are not just prettier names for a hard-coded XYZ point.

This is the important rule: use an anchor when you need to describe a relationship or semantic mounting reference. Do not add anchors to every component pre-emptively.

5. Which kind of anchor?

Situation Use
Normal rectangular face/corner is enough Anchor.LEFT, Anchor.FRONT_TOP_RIGHT, etc.
The reusable part owns a special mounting point and orientation Named AnchorFrame returned by the component’s anchors()
The reference must follow a particular native edge/corner topology AnchorTopology
The reference exists only because of this larger assembly Assembly-owned with_anchor(), not an application-specific anchor added to the generic part

Start with the simplest standard Anchor. Move to AnchorFrame or AnchorTopology only when a face/corner reference cannot express the actual mounting intent.

6. Let SolidCraft own the native relationship

Forge describes the relationship; SolidCraft owns the resulting native geometry, occurrence hierarchy and joint data. Forge is not intended to grow a second general mating solver. That is also why a meaningful attach() is preferable to Forge inventing increasingly clever coordinate corrections.

offset=(u, v) moves within the attachment plane, gap is normal distance between references, and angle is the relative turn around the attachment normal. These are relationship values, not a replacement global XYZ transform.

There are two useful attachment modes. Normal attach() uses the chosen references to determine the relationship and placement. Use attach(..., as_built=True) when both occurrences are already in the intended pose and SolidCraft should record that existing pose as a fixed assembly relationship instead of repositioning them.

7. A group is organisation, not a relationship 

frame = (left + right).group("Frame")

group("Frame") creates a real nested native component so the occurrences appear together in the SolidCraft browser hierarchy. Grouping does not mate, align or rotate the parts and does not replace attach().

Use a group when the collection itself is a useful named subassembly or browser unit. Do not create a group merely because two components touch.

A practical decision sequence

  1. Will these features be manufactured as one physical item? Keep them in one component, even if the geometry is complex.
  2. Is something installed or manufactured separately? Give it its own component occurrence.
  3. Do you only need a deliberate occurrence pose? Supply placement=Placement(...) when creating or copying it.
  4. Should one separate part follow another semantically? Use attach() and the simplest suitable anchor.
  5. Is a standard face/corner insufficient? Define an AnchorFrame or topology-backed reference at the level that owns that meaning.
  6. Do several occurrences form a useful named subassembly/browser unit? Then use group().

After this page, the Components and assemblies chapter covers parameter sharing, offsets, custom frames, topology anchors and assembly-owned datums in detail.

item.title: Geometry, sketches and Boolean operations
item.description:
Start with a solid

Box, Cylinder and Sphere are centred on their geometric CENTER by default. Use anchor=... when a face, axial end or tangent datum should lie at the origin. For Cylinder the anchor is resolved after choosing Axis.X, Axis.Y or Axis.Z; for example LEFT/RIGHT are the axial ends of an X-axis cylinder and BOTTOM/TOP are the axial ends of a Z-axis cylinder.

from scpf import (
 BOTTOM, FRONT, LEFT, RIGHT,
 Axis, Box, Cylinder, Sphere,
)

plate = Box(80, 50, 8)
board = Box(80, 50, 12).at(
 0, 0, 0,
 anchor=FRONT + BOTTOM,
).fillet(
 4,
 edges=[BOTTOM + LEFT, BOTTOM + RIGHT],
)
pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.Z).at(
 10, 10, 8,
 anchor=BOTTOM,
)
side_pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at(-10, 0, 0)
ball = Sphere(12)

body = Sphere(20) & Box(30, 30, 30)
centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body)

at(x, y, z) places CENTER at those coordinates unless another anchor=... is supplied. Passing another Shape instead uses shape-relative CENTER-to-CENTER placement. Forge derives the native Box corner, Cylinder base or Sphere center from the selected datum; callers do not add manual half-size corrections.

Draw a 2D profile, then extrude it

A Rectangle2D is a planar profile rather than a 3D body. 2D geometry is authored inside an explicit Sketch scope. Polygon2D can be created on the XY, XZ or YZ plane.

from scpf import Sketch, Rectangle2D, Polygon2D

with Sketch(plane="XY") as plate_sketch:
 Rectangle2D(80, 50)
plate = plate_sketch.extrude(8)

with Sketch(plane="XZ") as side_sketch:
 Polygon2D(
 [(0, 0), (40, 0), (40, 8), (8, 8), (8, 30), (0, 30)],
 plane="XZ",
 world=True,
 )
side = side_sketch.extrude(10)

# Signed distance chooses the side of the sketch plane.
backward = plate_sketch.extrude(-8)
centered = plate_sketch.extrude(8, sym=True)

A sketch plane affects where its axes go; changing the camera does not rotate its geometry. Leave the with Sketch(...) scope, then call sketch.extrude(...) to create 3D material. A positive distance follows the sketch-plane normal, a negative distance goes the other way, and sym=True divides a positive distance equally over both sides. Direct Rectangle2D(...).extrude(...) syntax is intentionally not supported.

Polygon2D works in standalone explicit Sketches and in face-attached explicit Sketches; its authored vertices stay sketch-local. Standalone Sketches may also use an explicit origin= and rotation=(rx, ry, rz). An extrusion from that rotated local frame can participate directly in +, - or & CSG, including non-axis-aligned cutters.

Select profiles when extruding a Sketch

By default Sketch.extrude() uses every closed profile in the Sketch. Use profiles=[(x, y), ...] when only some closed regions should be extruded or cut. The points are fixed coordinates in the Sketch itself; users do not need SolidCraft profile indices or curve ids.

from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Circle2D, Depth, Sketch

board = Box(120, 80, 5, anchor=Anchor.BOTTOM)
with Sketch(name="Selected holes", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as holes:
 seed = holes.add(Circle2D(d=8), offset=(-30, 0))
 holes.rectangular_pattern(
 seed,
 count=4,
 spacing=20,
 direction=Axis.X,
 )

board = board - holes.extrude(
 Depth.THROUGH_ALL,
 profiles=[(-30, 0), (-10, 0), (30, 0)],
 exact_regions=True,
)

SolidCraft 0.42 stores a successful point selection using the curves around the selected profile where possible. That lets the selection follow the profile when the saved design recomputes. exact_regions=True asks SolidCraft to use exactly the region containing each point. Profile points must be fixed finite numbers; Forge Parameters and expressions are not accepted in this field.

Repeat and mirror profiles inside one Sketch

Sketch.rectangular_pattern() makes a native SolidCraft sketch pattern from a profile that already belongs to the Sketch. Sketch.mirror() mirrors a profile, a pattern result or an earlier mirror result. Both methods return a Sketch result that can be passed to another supported Sketch operation.

from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Circle2D, Depth, Sketch

board = Box(200, 120, 8)
with Sketch(name="Dog holes", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as holes:
 seed = holes.add(Circle2D(d=8), offset=(-40, 20))
 row = holes.rectangular_pattern(
 seed,
 count=4,
 spacing=25,
 direction=Axis.X,
 )
 holes.mirror(row, axis=Axis.X)

board = board - holes.extrude(Depth.THROUGH_ALL)

The same operations work with native Slot profiles. A pattern or mirror result can be used as the source of the next operation.

from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Sketch, SlotCenterToCenter2D

with Sketch(name="Clamp slots", on=board, parent=Anchor.TOP) as slots:
 seed = SlotCenterToCenter2D((20, 20), (40, 20), 8)
 arm = slots.rectangular_pattern(
 seed,
 count=2,
 spacing=50,
 direction=Axis.X,
 )
 opposite = slots.mirror(arm, axis=Axis.Y)
 slots.mirror(arm, axis=Axis.X)
 slots.mirror(opposite, axis=Axis.X)

count, count2, spacing and spacing2 may use suitable model Parameters, so those values remain editable in the saved SolidCraft design. Current native qualification covers attached Sketch(on=...) use. Pattern directions support Axis.X, Axis.Y or a fixed 2D vector. Mirrors currently support the Sketch X or Y origin axis. Per-instance pattern suppression is not supported.

SolidCraft 0.42 stores the curves selected when a mirror is created. If a pattern later creates extra curves after its count changes, those new curves are not added to that existing mirror automatically.

Add, subtract and intersect 

body = Box(50, 50, 20)
tool = Cylinder(d=12, h=22).at(0, 0, 0)
joined = body + tool # union, where supported
cut = body - tool # difference, where supported
shared = body & tool # intersection, where supported

The supported compiler path depends on the operands. Native feature history and CSG trees are not interchangeable for every operation. For manufacturing features such as holes, prefer the native feature operations.

item.title: Getting started
item.description:
What SCPF does

SCPF is a Python interface and compiler for native SolidCraft commands. It is not a replacement CAD kernel. You describe a model using ordinary Python; SolidCraft executes the generated commands and owns the final geometry and feature history.

Install the library

In the lib.py.solidcraft.forge repository and an active Python environment:

python -m pip install -e ./scpf
python -m unittest discover -s scpf/tests -v

Your first model

Define one class, give it numeric dimensions, and return the body from build(). No main() or show() is necessary.

from scpf import Box, Edges

class Plate:
 length = 100.0
 width = 60.0
 thickness = 10.0

 def build(self):
 plate = Box(self.length, self.width, self.thickness)
 return plate.fillet(2, edges=Edges.VERTICAL)

Plate()

Compile, inspect, then execute

Save the model as model.py. Compilation alone does not open SolidCraft. The JSON is a native command plan, not a mesh or STEP file.

python -m scpf model.py --out output/model.json
python -m json.tool output/model.json

For a live GUI run, open SolidCraft, enable Preferences → Assistant → Let AI agents connect, and use:

python -m scpf model.py --connect --new

--new asks SolidCraft to replace the active design with a new, empty one before the model batch is sent. Leave it off when you deliberately want to add commands to the current design. Neither form saves the design. The CAD project also provides a separate native CLI qualification workflow.

Where to continue

Read Model objects first. Then read Positioning and orientation. That chapter explains the practical difference between at(), on(), Shape.attach(), Placement and Occurrence.attach(). After that, From one component to an assembly shows how separate physical parts are combined.

item.title: Model objects and parameters
item.description:
A model is a normal Python class

Numeric class attributes become editable SolidCraft parameters when SCPF compiles a plain model class. build() returns geometry. If a file contains exactly one public class with build(), that class is the root automatically; no trailing constructor call or launcher file is needed.

from scpf import Box

class Plate:
 length = 100.0
 width = 60.0
 thickness = 10.0

 def build(self):
 return Box(self.length, self.width, self.thickness)

Run that source file directly with python -m scpf plate.py --connect. The same rule lets a reusable component file serve as its standalone model while assemblies import the exact same class. If a file contains several public model classes, SCPF deliberately does not guess: finish the script with an explicit call such as Assembly() to choose the root.

An explicit final call is also how you override root parameters for a particular run, for example Plate(width=80). Arithmetic such as self.length / 2 is preserved symbolically for supported expressions; general Python computations are not automatically made parametric.

Parameter intent is visible in the name

SCPF distinguishes three kinds of numeric class attributes. This keeps a Python build setting from looking like a native editable CAD parameter.

class Display:
 PANEL_COUNT = 5 # fixed constant
 _panel_pitch = 160.0 # Forge/build-time input
 opening_width = 844.0 # native model parameter
Name Meaning SolidCraft parameter
UPPER_CASE Fixed constant No
_lower_case Forge/build-time input No
lower_case Editable model parameter Yes

If a public lower-case parameter is consumed only as a concrete Python value—for example through pv()—Forge emits a ModelParameterWarning. The same warning is emitted when a parameter remains native in some geometry but is also flattened into concrete occurrence placement. Such a parameter is only partly associative: editing it in SolidCraft would update only part of the model. Keep Placement coordinates symbolic or rename an intentionally build-time input with a leading underscore.

Share one model parameter across child components

Passing a parent parameter into several component inputs keeps one native SolidCraft parameter instead of creating component-specific duplicates.

bottom = BottomBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius)
roof = RoofBoard(corner_radius=self.corner_radius)
bracket = Bracket(
 bracket_width=self.bracket_width,
 inside_corner_radius=self.corner_radius,
)

Here the wooden fillets and bracket inside fillet all depend on the same corner_radius. Passing the parent parameter into the child input reuses that existing native dependency rather than creating a duplicate child parameter.

Reusable component defaults stay fixed unless they are explicitly published with include=. Parent Parameters/Expressions passed into child inputs always stay symbolic and reuse the existing parent dependency.

Bracket = component(
 CornerBracket,
 include=("inside_corner_radius",),
)

# Or publish all public defaults explicitly:
FullyEditableBracket = component(CornerBracket, include="*")

This publication rule is recorded in change 0003.

Shape versus component occurrence

Shape describes geometry or a feature expression (Box, Hole, an extrusion). A component occurrence is one placed instance of a shared, editable model definition. Do not confuse a new occurrence with a new feature history.

from scpf import Box, Placement, component

class Block:
 def build(self):
 return Box(40, 20, 10)

BlockComponent = component(Block)
first = BlockComponent(placement=Placement(x=-25))
second = first.copy(placement=Placement(x=25))
assembly = first + second

The two occurrences share the same Block definition. Placement is occurrence creation metadata: XYZ is absolute in the parent coordinate frame and optional rotation adds orientation. The component definition never receives placement as a model parameter.

Groups are actual native parent components 

blocks = (first + second).group("Blocks")

Grouping changes the browser hierarchy, not the geometry’s orientation. At present one shared definition cannot be split among different groups.

Important boundaries

Associative attachment is supported for a limited set of rectangular component faces. General mates, arbitrary face queries and rotational constraints are not implemented as a complete assembly solver.

Next:Positioning and orientation explains how to place geometry and component occurrences, and when at(), on() or attach() is the right choice.

item.title: Positioning and orientation
item.description:
Which one do I use?

These APIs all affect where something ends up, but they mean different things. Choose the one that matches the rule in the model.

You want to… Use What it means
Place or align geometry inside one part shape.at(...) Geometric placement. No joint or assembly relationship is created.
Put a feature on a face of another shape feature.on(...) Within-part feature placement. The selected Faces value chooses the support or entry face.
Place a feature with explicit parent/child anchors Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring. Prefer on() when a simple face is enough.
Give one component occurrence an absolute pose Placement(...) Position and optional orientation at occurrence creation/copy time. No joint is created.
Relate two separate physical component occurrences Occurrence.attach(...) An assembly relationship that SolidCraft stores as a native joint.

The important distinction:Shape.attach() and Occurrence.attach() have the same verb but work at different levels. The first places a feature inside one part. The second relates two separate component occurrences.

Start with the coordinate system

X, Y and Z are model axes. A normal Box has its large base in XY and thickness along Z. A camera rotation changes only the view. It does not change the model coordinates.

Also separate two levels: geometry inside one part has its own coordinates; a component occurrence has a pose in the assembly.

Use at() to place or align geometry 

from scpf import Anchor, Axis, Box, Cylinder

pin = Cylinder(d=8, h=20, axis=Axis.X).at(
 10, 0, 5,
 anchor=Anchor.LEFT,
)

body = Box(80, 50, 12)
centered_bore = Cylinder(d=8, h=30, axis=Axis.X).at(body)

shape.at(x, y, z) places supported geometry at an absolute model coordinate. A primitive can use anchor=... to say which of its own datums belongs at that coordinate.

shape.at(target) currently aligns CENTER to CENTER. It does not mean “put this on the top face”. For a feature on a face, use on().

Use on() for a feature on a face 

from scpf import Box, Depth, Faces, Hole

plate = Box(100, 60, 10)
hole = Hole(d=8, depth=Depth.THROUGH_ALL).on(
 plate,
 face=Faces.TOP,
 offset=(20, 0),
)
plate = plate + hole

on() is for a feature that belongs to an existing shape. Faces.TOP or Faces.BOTTOM selects the face where the feature starts or is supported. The offset is measured in that face.

A sketch has the same idea in explicit form: Sketch(on=body, parent=Anchor.TOP) creates a named sketch on a selected body face.

Shape.attach() is lower-level within-part placement 

from scpf import Anchor, Boss, X, Y

boss = Boss(d=7, h=12, hole_d=2.5).attach(
 case,
 parent=Anchor.INNER_BOTTOM,
 offset=(X.MIN + 10, Y.MAX - 10),
)

Use Shape.attach() only when a simple on() face does not express the required feature reference. It lets you choose explicit parent and child anchors.

This does not create an assembly joint. The feature and target are still geometry inside one part.

Use Placement for a component occurrence 

from scpf import Placement, X, Z, component

@component
class Panel:
 def build(self):
 return Box(160, 320, 14.5)

first = Panel()
second = first.copy(
 placement=Placement(x=160, z=20)
)

upright = first.copy(
 placement=Placement(
 z=160,
 rotation=(X, 90),
 )
)

upside_down = first.copy(
 placement=Placement(rotation=(Z, 180))
)

Placement describes the complete pose of one component occurrence in its parent coordinate frame. XYZ is absolute. The optional rotation is one axis-angle orientation.

Placement does not say that one component depends on another. It only says where this occurrence is.

Use Occurrence.attach() for separate physical parts 

from scpf import Anchor

left = Block()
right = Block().attach(
 left,
 parent=Anchor.RIGHT,
 child=Anchor.LEFT,
)

assembly = left + right

Here right is a separate physical part. Its rule is not an absolute XYZ position; its left side belongs on the right side of left. That is an assembly relationship, so use Occurrence.attach().

SolidCraft stores this as a native joint. If the parent changes size, the relationship can still express which references belong together. The next chapter, From one component to an assembly, builds on this distinction.

Shape.move() is a local geometry translation 

body = Box(40, 20, 10)
shifted = body.move(x=10, y=0, z=25)

move() translates supported geometry inside its current shape expression. It is not the normal way to position a component occurrence. Use Placement for occurrences.

Copies can have different placements 

first = Panel(
 placement=Placement(z=160, rotation=(X, 90))
)
second = first.copy(
 placement=Placement(x=160, z=160, rotation=(X, 90))
)
screen = first + second

The two occurrences reuse one component definition but have different placements. copy() without a placement override keeps the source Placement.

Current limits

Operation Current meaning
Shape.at(...) Absolute geometry placement; shape-to-shape alignment is currently CENTER-to-CENTER.
Shape.on(...) Supported within-part feature placement on TOP or BOTTOM.
Shape.attach(...) Lower-level within-part feature anchoring.
Placement(...) Absolute occurrence pose with one optional axis-angle rotation.
Occurrence.attach(...) Assembly relationship between separate component occurrences.

item.title: Sheet metal
item.description:
Sheet metal is native editable history

Forge sheet-metal operations lower to SolidCraft sheet rules and native sheet features. Use them when the saved design must keep material thickness, bend allowance and a recoverable flat pattern. Do not replace these operations with fused solid envelopes when native history matters.

One sheet rule owns the material

A sheet body has one active rule. That rule owns thickness, k_factor and the default bend_radius. Operations on an existing sheet inherit those values instead of restating them. Feature-specific dimensions such as flange height, hem length or a path-flange radius override remain on the feature.

Create a flat sheet body 

with Sketch(name="Blank", plane="XY") as sketch:
 Rectangle2D(80, 40)

sheet = sketch.sheet_metal(
 thickness=2,
 bend_radius=2,
 k_factor=0.5,
 rule_name="Panel sheet",
)

Sketch.sheet_metal() creates a new sheet body from one closed Sketch. It is a body-creation operation, not a feature applied to an existing sheet.

Fold existing material 

sheet = sheet.fold(
 line=((20, -20, 0), (20, 20, 0)),
 angle=90,
 fixed=(-30, 0, 0),
)

Shape.fold() bends material that already belongs to the sheet. The initial contract uses one straight fixed-coordinate fold line. Thickness, K-factor and bend radius come from the active rule.

Grow an edge flange 

sheet = sheet.flange(
 edges=[(40, 0, 2)],
 height=20,
 angle=90,
)

Shape.flange() adds material to explicit existing sheet edges. Height and angle may remain parameterized. Edge selection is currently a non-empty set of fixed XYZ pick points; generic topology selectors are not yet part of this API.

Create a sheet from an open contour 

with Sketch(name="Contour", plane="XZ") as sketch:
 chain = sketch.chain(start=(0, 0))
 chain.line_to((35, 0))
 chain.tangent_arc_to((40, 5))
 chain.line_to((40, 30))
 contour = chain.finish()

sheet = contour.contour_flange(
 distance=50,
 thickness=2.5,
 bend_radius=2.5,
 k_factor=0.44,
)

Shape.contour_flange() is the other body-creation operation. Its receiver is a finished connected open Sketch chain. Forge preserves chain order and replay-bound native curve identity; callers do not pass SolidCraft curve ids.

Hem an existing edge 

sheet = sheet.hem(
 edges=[(40, 0, 2)],
 length=12,
 gap=4,
)

Shape.hem() folds an existing edge back onto the sheet while inheriting the active material rule. The first contract uses fixed XYZ edge picks. Length and optional gap are feature dimensions and may be parameterized.

Follow a reusable path 

with Sketch(name="Path", plane="XZ") as sketch:
 chain = sketch.chain(start=(0, 0))
 chain.line_to((0, 14))
 path = chain.finish()

sheet = sheet.path_flange(
 edge=(40, 0, 2),
 path=path,
 radius=3,
)

Shape.path_flange() adds a native flange to an existing edge using a finished open Sketch path. The qualified SolidCraft 0.45 contract is line-only. Omitting radius inherits the active rule; supplying it overrides only this feature’s bend radius.

Apply a whole-sheet perforation field 

sheet = sheet.perforate(
 diameter=5,
 pitch=10,
 margin=5,
 pattern="square",
)

Shape.perforate() adds native manufacturing perforation semantics to existing sheet material. Diameter and pitch are positive millimetre dimensions. margin is optional; omitting it leaves SolidCraft’s native diameter-sized margin default in control. pattern is staggered by default or may be square.

The first Forge contract applies to the whole sheet. It deliberately does not expose SolidCraft’s Sketch/profile-bounded region fields. Perforations remain flat-pattern/DXF/measurement semantics rather than repeated B-rep holes.

Editable dimensions versus topology picks

Keep design dimensions symbolic when the method accepts Parameter/Expression values. Current edge picks and straight fold-line coordinates are intentionally fixed finite coordinates. Forge rejects unsupported associative selectors instead of pretending a numeric pick is a stable topology reference.

Verification and flat patterns

Native sheet-metal verification is stronger than matching a formed bounding box. Verification cases inspect sheet-rule values, native bend/history records, saved-design parameter edits and the recoverable flat pattern. See the Verification catalog, especially the Sheet metal group.

item.title: Verification and API boundaries
item.description:
Unit tests for Python behavior

The library’s tests under scpf/tests/ cover model objects, feature compilation, reusable components and rotation validation. For example, an occurrence rotation test checks that the compiler emits one occurrence.move with the expected native parameters.

python -m unittest discover -s scpf/tests -v

Test compiled native commands

Compare the generated command structure with explicit expectations, not only with a count of operations. Tests should check component names, requested positions, the orientation axis and angle, and feature ordering. A regression can preserve a known good JSON fixture when command ordering is part of the contract.

Native geometric verification

The CAD model repository runs a separate SolidCraft CLI workflow for native geometry, editable history, STEP output, measurements and screenshots. Read the saved SolidCraft occurrence transforms, not just whether a command ran successfully. A valid Python object or syntactically valid command plan is not evidence that the final solid occupies the correct plane or has no collision.

Keep implementation and docs in sync

When placement syntax changes, add tests for the exact generated native commands before documenting it as supported. Named principal-axis rotation is supported; chained rotations are still not.

For a plain-language explanation of the implementation and its boundaries, read How SCPF works (without building a second CAD engine).
